text: The assembly will hear an address by His
Excellency Philip Edward Davis,
Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of
the Bahamas.
I request protocol
to escort his excellency and invite him

Mr. President,
Mr. Secretary General,
excellencies, distinguished delegates,
congratulations, your excellency Khalila

Mr. President, every generation inherits
a promise it did not make.
The promise of our generation was made
81 years ago with the foundation the
founding of this United Nations from the
ashes of the worst war in human history.
Its ideals have proven its worth. No
nation is too small to be sovereign, no
people too poor to be equal. and the
strong should be bound by the same law
as the weak.
Sad to say, United Nations has drifted
from its promise. The Bahamas comes
today to insist on it.
Mr. President,
all week we've been told this is an age
of uncertainty.
With respect, I do not agree.
Uncertainty is the language of those who
have already decided and do not wish to
say so.
Treaties are being torn up. Institutions
are being starved. Rules are giving way
to deals. And the benefits of the deals
go to whoever holds the most leverage.
Once again, we hear the language of
spheres of influence of backyards and
hemispheres. For 500 years, the
Caribbean was somebody's backyard.
We did not win our freedom to once again
become somebody's backyard.
The message to small nations is very
clear.
Be as sovereign as we allow you to be.
Mr. President, a sovereignty that must
ask permission is not sovereignty.
It is a lease.
Our ancestors
did not break their chain so that their
children could become tenants.
These are not uncertain times.
These times are very certain. The only
uncertain thing is how we respond to the
opportunities and challenges of this
time.
People often say that the world lacks
political will. I do not agree. The
world has never lacked political will.
In 2008, when the banks of the richest
nations were failing, trillions of
dollars were found in a matter of weeks.
When a global pandemic reached the
capitals of the powerful, the political
will returned.
The will exists. It is simply pointed
elsewhere.
Somewhere a bank is always too big to
fail. Similarly, a nation should never
be too small to be left behind.
What the world lacks is not political
will for change. It is political change
itself.
A change in who writes the rules. A
change in whose suffering counts. A
change in who decides and who pays.
Political will is a feeling.
Political change is a decision about who
holds the power. And Mr. President, that
is what I have come to speak about
today. Power.
Two and a half thousand years ago, the
envoys of Athens stood before the small
island of Milos and told his people a
simple truth about power. The strong
will do what they can. The weak will
suffer what they must.
81 years ago in San Francisco, humanity
wrote a different law. The sovereign
equality of nations,

of standing. The United Nations was the

nearly one in three people on Earth
still lived under colonial rule. The

The Bahamas was not in that room, but we
were on the map. Then came political
change for us. Not granted from above,
demanded from below. And so on the 18th
of September 1973, the Bahamas took its
seat in this assembly.
Then in 1985,
commerce leaders met in my own capital
and agreed a Nassau accord against
apathide.

Less than five years later, Nelson
Mandela walked free.
None of that happened because the
powerful suddenly found their
conscience. It happened because the
balance of power in the room was
changed.
That is the lesson of history. Change is
not given.
It is organized.
It is not the small states who are
dismantling the rules-based order.
Small countries cannot dismantle a
rules-based world. But we will be the
first to be crushed beneath its
collapse.
Great powers can survive the end of the
rules. Small states cannot. For us, a
rulesbased world is our shield. The
rules have not always been applied
fairly, but the answer is not a world
without rules. It is rules that bind the
strong as firmly as the weak.
International order, where rules apply
only to the weak, is not order. It is a
hierarchy.
When the Bahamas defends
multilateralism,
we're not defending a bureaucracy.
We're defending the only successful
arrangement in which a nation of 400,000
people can stand at this position as the
sovereign equal of a nation of a billion
people. A world without rules is not a
free world. It is me loss.
Mr. President,
I do not appeal to conscience. Small
states have done that for decades.
Today I appeal to your interests.
What is in your best interest?
No wall is high enough to keep out
rising warming seas. No border strong
enough to stop a pandemic.
Narrow self-interests ask what you can
take today. Enlightened self-interests
ask what kind of world you will have to
live in tomorrow.
The national base rule-based order it
benefits all. They're not arbitrary
having been arrived at through lived
experience.
Every rule you break today is a rule you
will need tomorrow. Every institution
you starve is one you will one one day
call upon.
Every small nation you abandon is a
crisis you will one day inherit.
Defending the rules is not a favor to
the small. It is an insurance for the
strong.
Mr. President,
nowhere is that truer than the climate

lives by next February.

Families watched the sea, take the only
land they had. Most of my country sits
barely above sea level. For us, a rising

boundary inching towards our doorsteps.
That is why the Bahamas proudly endorses

rise, which affirms that our statethood,

People who lose their homes do not

Mr. President,
the next context for power will not only
be fought over land and sea, it will be
fought over data.
Our citizens data crosses the world
without a visa and without a vote. It
leaves our shores as raw material and
returns as products we must buy. We have
seen this pattern before.
My islands once exported salt, sponge
and cyo. Others set the price. Others
kept the profit. The commodity was has

This is colonization by data.
it serve. It does not arrive with ships

dominating languages and dominating

And it means taking part in the digital
age on our own terms. Not as consumers
of other people's systems, but as
builders of our own.
Data is the newest raw material in the
global economy. My friends, the old
empires took our lands, plundered them,
and renamed them. The new ones seek to
take our data and hand us back a picture
of ourselves, one we did not paint. In
this modern age, are we expected to be
simply the unquestioning supplies of
data? Or can we not rightly expect to
participate in processing our own data
so as to refine it, govern it, and
profit from it?
We do not think it outrageous to demand
that small states help the rules of this

international telecommunication union a

that we have what I call data
sovereignty.

ended 81 years ago.
The world has changed. The council has
not. Five nations still hold a veto over
the peace of 193.

None of us was asked.
An institution that cannot reform itself
cannot hope to reform the world.
[applause]

the Bahamas seeks a seat on the council

to help change it. A council that

a table where our survival is decided.
Change must also reach the leadership of

Mr. President,
the founders of this organization
made their promise
in the ruins of war.
We should not need ruins to find our own
